feedback: If the learner places a species by overall resemblance rather than a specific shared character, ask which single trait marks the branch they chose and whether the species actually has it.
When placement is correct, confirm the shared derived character that defines that branch (e.g. 'feathers appear at this node, so everything beyond it shares that ancestor').

Note that only shared DERIVED characters define a clade; a trait inherited from an older ancestor and also found in animals outside the group (an ancestral trait) does not pinpoint close relationship.
activities.intendedInsight: A cladogram is built from shared derived characters: in a simple classroom tree, a marked node shows where a new trait is assumed to have appeared in a common ancestor and been passed on to its descendants (some may later lose it), so species group by shared ancestry evidenced by shared derived features.
learnerActions: Use a character matrix or checklist (feathers? teeth? three-toed foot?) and tick which traits a mystery animal has.

Place the animal onto the branch defined by the shared derived characters (newer traits) it has in common with others, so grouping follows those shared derived features, not overall physical resemblance or left-to-right order.
Add a new species to a partially completed cladogram using only its listed features, then explain which shared character justifies its position.
activities.title: Build the tree from a character checklist

feedback: If the learner names an internal node's identity wrongly, remind them the node stands for a shared ancestor, not one of the species shown at the tips (which may be living or extinct).
If they pick the pair drawn side by side, have them trace both pairs to their joining nodes and compare which node is more recent.
Reinforce that a pair whose lines meet at a more recent node (closer to the tips) is more closely related than a pair whose lines meet only at the base.
activities.intendedInsight: Relatedness is read as 'most recent common ancestor', found by tracing branches down to the node where two lines meet — a central tree-reading skill.
learnerActions: Pick two species (e.g. a shark and a lizard) and trace the lines down each branch until they meet at a node.
State that the meeting node is their most recent common ancestor and that this, not tip nearness, sets how closely related they are.
Given three species, decide which two are most closely related by comparing where each pair's branches join.
activities.title: Trace two tips to their most recent common ancestor

feedback: If the learner still chooses adjacent tips, trace each pair back to its branching node together and compare the depths of those nodes.
Confirm success when the learner cites the more recent shared node rather than side-by-side placement.

Address the related error that the top/far-right species is 'most advanced': each tip has its own mix of older and newer traits, and in dinosaur trees many tips are extinct species from different times, so a tip's position does not show it is more advanced.
activities.intendedInsight: Physical closeness of tips on the page does not indicate relatedness; only the recency of the shared ancestor (node) does.
learnerActions: Examine a layout where two animals are drawn right next to each other but their traced lines only meet at the very base of the tree.
Find an animal drawn far across the page whose line meets one of them at a much more recent node.
Decide and explain which animals are actually most closely related, justifying the answer by the branching, not the page position.
activities.title: The trap: nearest tip is not the closest relative

feedback: If the learner thinks rotation changed relationships, have them re-trace the same pair to the same node before and after rotating.
Confirm understanding when they state that the order of tips is arbitrary and no tip is 'higher' or more evolved than another.
Reinforce that on a cladogram the ancestors are the internal nodes, not the tips; every tip, living or extinct, is drawn as a branch end, not as the ancestor of another tip.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree encodes branching order (ancestry), not left-right layout; orientation is arbitrary and rotating at a node preserves all relationships.
learnerActions: Rotate a node so the tips swing to new left-right positions.
Re-trace two previously compared tips and confirm their meeting node — and so their relatedness — is unchanged.
Explain in their own words why rotating a branch, or the left-to-right order of tips, does not change which species are most closely related.
activities.title: Rotate a branch and check what stays the same
